parts.summary: Build a simple attendance website for the department’s teachers and students. Students check in on phones; teachers manage attendance on laptops.
parts.details:
The department has about 40 teachers and 1,200 students. Target a supervised class pilot for the week-6 demo, with wider rollout dependent on school approval and capacity testing. A department-wide launch is not established by one successful demo.

Adam owns browser behaviour, Sara owns server logic and data, and Yassine owns page layout, usability and test coordination. Keep the appearance close to the school’s pages.

Use only free resources. Before using real student records, confirm that storage, backups and any logs containing student data remain in the EU. Confirm a usable hosting route and school Wi-Fi access in week 1. If these are unresolved, demonstrate with invented records and clearly report that real use is blocked.

parts.summary: Keep all four attendance essentials. Plan 100 hours of work and protect 44 hours for uncertainty and fixes. Show a working attendance flow by the end of week 3.
parts.details: Day one includes opening a class session, accepting student check-ins for its first 10 minutes, updating the teacher’s list automatically, recording teacher corrections and exporting CSV. CSV is a table file that spreadsheet tools can open. Minimum supporting work includes approved user identification, class membership, duplicate prevention and clear failure messages. Defer statistics, absence emails and a native phone app. They add work without completing the core attendance flow. Use school-supplied class lists; defer a class-management interface. Weeks 1–2: resolve hosting and identity, agree data exchanged between pages and server, and build with invented records. Week 3: demonstrate opening a session, checking in and seeing the list update. Weeks 4–5: complete corrections, export and integration. Week 6: testing, fixes and demo only. checklist.answer: Build a simple attendance website where department students check in by phone and teachers manage attendance on laptops.
Keep sessions, the 10-minute check-in window, automatic list updates, teacher corrections and CSV. Defer statistics, alerts, native apps and class-management screens to protect the core workflow.

Adam: 4+10+10+4+6=34 hours. Sara: 5+6+8+6+3+5=33. Yassine: 4+10+5+4+6+4=33. Total: 100 hours. Reserve: 144−100=44 hours, or 30.6% of capacity. Capacity estimates and failure-state tests use existing task allowances. Fit remains conditional on straightforward approved identity, hosting and test setup.
By day 21, demonstrate a teacher opening a session, a student checking in and the teacher's list updating. Use invented records unless real-data approval is complete.
Each task names exactly one owner in its title and one work area in its area field. Sara owns capacity work; the architect reviews it.
Adam owns JavaScript behaviour, Sara owns Python/SQL and deployment, and Yassine owns HTML/CSS presentation and test coordination. Keep presentation files separate from behaviour files.

Agree data exchange and sample responses in the first two days. Adam and Yassine can build independently of the server. Resolve external school dependencies in week 1; unresolved approval blocks real use, but not a synthetic-data demo.
All three have substantial work within their 48-hour limits. Adam retains 14 hours; Sara and Yassine retain 15 each.
Demo by day 42, in week 6. Finish planned features by day 35. Keep week 6 for checks, fixes and rehearsal; confirm each person's weekly availability.

Sara watches hosting, identity, storage and measured capacity. Adam watches integration and scope. Yassine watches school Wi-Fi, device usability and acceptance results, including failure states and manual fallback.
Use one shared task board, a short weekly review, a week-3 demonstration and a week-6 acceptance checklist. This is enough process for three people and six weeks.

Do not promise department-wide readiness within this budget or assume any free host meets EU requirements. Start with a supervised pilot. Confirm EU hosting and compare measured workload and storage needs with server capacity before real use.

parts.summary: Use one Django website with HTML/CSS, small JavaScript files and PostgreSQL. Hosting is conditional on free school-provided infrastructure in the EU.
parts.details: Django is a Python framework with built-in accounts, forms and database tools. It fits Sara’s Python/SQL; Adam handles browser updates; Yassine builds templates and styles. The proposed shared plan below totals 100 hours, including 12 learning hours and four setup hours. It replaces overlapping manager tasks; it is not an extra architecture budget. Adam owns 36 hours, Sara 35 and Yassine 29, leaving 44 of 144 hours protected. The manager’s detailed plan was not supplied, so exact reconciliation needs confirmation. Use one repository and deployment. Drop React, a separate frontend, microservices and Kubernetes. Ask school IT in week 1 for free EU hosting, HTTPS and backups. Render’s free database expires after 30 days; its website can sleep. [Render limits](https://render.com/docs/free). If school hosting is unavailable, demonstrate with fictional data and leave deployment unresolved.

parts.summary: The browser talks to one application. Teacher lists refresh every five seconds. The server controls the ten-minute window and preserves the joining destination through sign-in.
parts.details: Modules cover accounts, rosters, sessions, attendance and CSV export. Students enter a code or open a session link. If sign-in is needed, preserve the destination using a validated local return path. Successful sign-in returns to that session; the server rechecks enrollment and deadline before check-in. A closed session explains that check-in ended and directs the student to the teacher. Wrong-class access reveals no roster and offers code re-entry. Yassine includes these states and expired-login recovery in the screen plan. Repeated submissions return the existing result; teacher corrections survive retries. Only teacher lists poll; stop when hidden and show stale/error status. Codes cannot prove physical presence. Pure functions handle timing, eligibility, corrections and CSV safety. Thin request handlers read time and records, call those functions and save results. Database constraints prevent duplicates. Split files before roughly 400 lines and reuse shared rules.
parts.diagram:
Student phone -- code/link --> session destination
Sign-in if needed --> preserved destination --> enrollment/deadline checks
Teacher laptop -- session / correction / export --> Django
Teacher laptop <-- list every 5 seconds -- Django
Django <--> PostgreSQL on approved EU hosting
PostgreSQL --> encrypted backup on separate EU storage

parts.summary: Keep minimal attendance records, change history and backups in the EU. Use fictional records for development.
parts.details: Tables: User, Class, TeacherAssignment, Enrollment, Session, Attendance and AttendanceChange. Store school identifier, display name, role, class membership, opening/closing times and attendance status. Attendance is unique per session/student. Snapshot the enrolled roster when opening a session so later roster edits do not rewrite history. Keep correction actor, time, previous value, new value and reason. Students see their own result; teachers access assigned classes only. Protect CSV exports using the same access checks and neutralize cells that spreadsheets could execute as formulas. Exports also contain student data: school-approved EU storage is required. Avoid location tracking, advertising tools and external assets. Keep personal data out of routine logs. Propose nightly encrypted database backups, seven daily copies and a restore test before the demo; school policy must approve retention for records, changes, logs, exports and backups.

Keep database credentials, login client secrets and signing keys in server environment settings or a secret store. Never commit them, send them to browsers or print them in logs.

Store school account ID, display name, role, class enrolment, session times, attendance and correction history. Students see their own result; teachers see assigned classes; authorised operators have limited operational access. All copies, logs and backups stay in the EU. The …

Check input types, lengths, allowed status values and permissions on the server. Use SQL placeholders, never joined query strings. Escape displayed text and neutralise spreadsheet formulas in CSV. Pass server time into small, pure deadline-rule functions for easy tests.
No public signup or self-selected teacher roles. Confirm school login abuse controls; limit app login starts and check-ins per account with network-wide safeguards that tolerate shared school Wi-Fi.

Use HTTPS for all pages, API calls and live connections. Use Secure, HttpOnly cookies so they travel only over HTTPS and cannot be read by page scripts. Configure SameSite cookies and protection against forged browser requests using the framework. Test …

A leak can reveal attendance patterns even without passwords. Minimise records, enforce retention, restrict database accounts and encrypt backups. On discovery, stop exposure, revoke affected sessions or secrets and notify the school's incident contact promptly for assessment and required notifications.

Phone check-in is not proof of presence. Free-only hosting may not satisfy EU-only handling. CSV creates extra copies. Use teacher review, verified hosting and restricted exports; demonstrate with invented data if prerequisites remain unresolved.

challenges.idea: CSV export is only a download feature.
challenges.problem: Downloads create uncontrolled copies and spreadsheet software may interpret student text as formulas.
challenges.better: Limit exports by class, neutralise formula cells and use the school's approved storage and retention rules.

parts.summary:
A simple website with four screens for student phones and teacher laptops.
Use familiar school styling, clear status messages and one main action per screen.
parts.details: Screens: (1) Teacher classes: choose a class and open its session. (2) Live register: show the session code, closing time, attendance, connection status, manual corrections and CSV export. (3) Student check-in: enter the code, confirm the class and remaining time, then press Check in. (4) Student result: confirm recorded attendance or explain why check-in failed. Students open the school-provided app address and sign in before entering a session code. Teachers read out or write the code on the board. Do not project the register. Defer QR generation, a separate joining display and name search. Use shared Django templates, ordinary JavaScript and CSS. Templates reuse page structure on the server. Adam handles browser behaviour; Yassine handles presentation and keyboard checks; Sara handles server responses that distinguish saving, saved and rejected actions. React is not a dependency. Keep this work to 20 hours within the shared 100-hour plan, not an additional allocation. …

decisions.title: How students reach a session

options.name: App address, sign-in, then session code
options.good: Works with a spoken or written code; needs no projector.
options.bad: Students must type the code and may make mistakes.
options.fit: Matches the architecture; no extra joining feature beyond its code flow.

options.name: Session link with optional QR code
options.good: Less typing when teachers can share or display it.
options.bad: Must preserve the session through login; QR adds generation and phone checks.
options.fit: Provisionally adds 3–5 implementation hours over code entry; not allocated.

decisions.picked: App address, sign-in, then session code
decisions.why: Use the architecture’s code submission flow. Sign-in comes first, so no session needs to survive login. Keep code errors on the same screen. Codes locate sessions; they do not prove identity or presence.

decisions.title: How teachers read attendance

options.name: Stable list with status text
options.good: Easy to scan; names stay in place during updates.
options.bad: Long classes require scrolling without name search.
options.fit: Fits laptops and the existing register scope.

options.name: Cards grouped by attendance
options.good: Separates present and absent groups clearly.
options.bad: Uses more space and moves students between groups.
options.fit: Adds layout work and increases correction mistakes.

decisions.why: Show counts above a fixed-order list. Label students without check-ins as Pending during the window. Defer name search; preserve focus when updates arrive.

decisions.title: How teachers repair a mistaken correction

options.name: Change and save the status again
options.good: Reuses the required correction control and server action.
options.bad: Takes another edit to reverse a mistake.
options.fit: Adam owns browser behaviour; Sara owns saving within the existing correction allocation.

options.name: Separate undo action
options.good: Quickly reverses the last change.
options.bad: Needs previous-value tracking and rules for intervening updates.
options.fit: Provisionally adds 2–4 implementation hours; defer because these are unallocated.

decisions.picked: Change and save the status again
decisions.why: Show the saved status clearly and keep it editable. This supports recovery without a second correction mechanism.

decisions.title: Visual foundation

options.name: Small shared school-style layout
options.good: Familiar appearance, reusable templates and no paid assets.
options.bad: The team must check contrast and keyboard behaviour.
options.fit: Uses Yassine’s HTML/CSS, Adam’s JavaScript and Sara’s Python.

options.name: Free CSS component library
options.good: Provides ready-made control styles.
options.bad: Adds learning and school-style adjustments.
options.fit: Only saves time if the team already knows it.

decisions.why: Use Django templates, ordinary browser controls, small JavaScript files and a shared stylesheet.

risks.risk: School Wi-Fi drops during check-in or a correction.
risks.action: Show saving until the server confirms. Preserve inputs on failure, offer retry and show the register’s last update time.

risks.risk: A live update moves a row during correction.
risks.action: Keep a stable order and keyboard focus. Show saved status and allow another correction.

risks.risk: Projecting the register exposes student attendance.
risks.action: Keep the register on the teacher’s laptop. Read out or write only the session code on the board.

tasks.title: Yassine: sketch four screens, code-entry flow and failure wording
Yassine: build shared responsive Django template markup and CSS
Adam: build student code-entry, check-in and result presentation
Adam: build teacher list and register presentation, including repeatable correction feedback
Yassine: check phones, keyboard, zoom and school Wi-Fi failure messages before week 6

checklist.answer: Students use phones; teachers use laptops. No projector is required. Teachers share the code verbally or on a board.
Four main screens: teacher classes opens sessions; live register manages attendance and export; student check-in accepts a code and confirms the class; result shows success or a recovery action.
Teacher: sign in → choose class → open session → manage register. Student: open app → sign in → enter code → confirm class and check in → see result. Identity method remains to be agreed.

Classes: no assigned classes, loading, retry. Register: missing roster or no check-ins, loading, disconnected; show correction/export errors. Check-in: blank code prompt, checking, invalid or closed session. Result: awaiting confirmation, recorded, or failed with retry/teacher fallback.

Use at least 16px body text, 44px primary touch targets and 4.5:1 normal-text contrast. Support keyboard use, visible focus and 200% zoom. Label fields, pair colour with text and announce action results without reading every live update.
Use a plain header, school colours, system fonts and simple lists. Request a school page reference. Serve assets with the EU-hosted app to avoid outside design-service requests.

Teacher screens share navigation and lists; student screens share a narrow panel. All reuse Django templates and CSS controls. These 20 hours use Yassine 12 and Adam 8 within the 100-hour plan. Sara owns server behaviour; authentication, integration and export …
A strict phone-only path excludes students with dead phones or Wi-Fi trouble. Show the exact ten-minute closing time and make teacher-recorded attendance the visible fallback.

challenges.idea: Every student checks in by phone during the first ten minutes.
challenges.problem: A dead phone, accessibility barrier or Wi-Fi failure can prevent a present student from recording attendance.
challenges.better: Keep the window, but support teacher-recorded attendance and explain this fallback on closed or failed check-in screens.

questions: Which school page should guide colours, language and layout?
How will users identify themselves, and where will class rosters come from?
How will students receive the app address before class?
What is the largest class, and are there known language or accessibility needs?
Does the shared 100-hour breakdown include these 20 hours and the existing code-entry and correction behaviour within each person’s 48-hour limit?

problems.problem: The 12 learning hours and local setup work are not mapped into the manager’s 100-hour plan. Adding them could consume the protected 30% buffer. Architecture tasks also lack individual owners.
problems.fix: Map each architecture task into the shared plan, assign Adam, Sara or Yassine as its sole owner, and explicitly budget learning and setup. Keep planned work at 100 hours or revise scope.

problems.problem: The 30 security hours are described as included, but there is no task mapping or named ownership proving this. Most work appears to fall on Sara, whose feature work already totals 33 hours.
problems.fix: Map the 30 hours to named tasks in the shared plan, identify overlaps, and check Sara’s total against her 48 hours while preserving the team buffer.

problems.problem: Local Django accounts are the architecture baseline, while security assumes school login. Secure initial password delivery, recovery, a suitable slow password hash and login-attempt limits remain unspecified for local accounts.
problems.fix: Agree one login route in week 1. If local accounts remain an option, specify school-managed provisioning and recovery, Argon2 password hashing and account-aware attempt limits; include their implementation hours.

problems.problem: The design relies on Adam’s React experience for shared screens, but the architecture explicitly selects Django templates and small JavaScript files. Following both plans could introduce an unbudgeted frontend stack.
problems.fix: Specify shared Django templates, ordinary JavaScript and CSS for the selected design. Remove React as an implementation dependency.

problems.problem: The selected QR/link flow does not match the architecture’s session-code submission flow. The team has no single agreement on how a student locates a session or returns to it after login.
problems.fix: Agree one joining flow with architecture: either a link that preserves the session through login, or explicit code entry. Compare the classroom effort and implementation hours before selecting it.

problems.problem: QR generation, a separate joining display, name search and an undo action add work beyond the four described screens. Their browser and server behaviour is not allocated in the shared plan.
problems.fix: Account for each addition within the 100-hour plan with one owner. Compare a typed link with QR support, and repeatable manual correction with undo; defer additions that do not fit.

problems.problem: The plan budgets deployment and peak-load checks without a provisional workload or storage estimate. Unknown class sizes are correctly questioned, but there is no measurable hosting acceptance target.
problems.fix: Have Sara and the architect define labelled workload assumptions, estimate attendance rows, backup storage and peak requests, and compare them with the school server’s confirmed capacity before approving real use.

problems.problem: The architecture introduces sign-in but does not explain its place in the student flow. An expired login could lose the joining destination and waste the ten-minute window.
problems.fix: Specify that successful sign-in returns students to the selected session, with clear handling for expired sessions and wrong-class access. Have Yassine include these states in the screen plan.

problems.problem: Acceptance testing has no explicit coverage for empty classes, loading lists, expired check-in windows or failed manual corrections. These states affect the day-one workflow on school Wi-Fi.
problems.fix: Add these cases to Yassine’s existing acceptance task, including preserved correction inputs, server-confirmed saves and a clear teacher-attendance fallback.

merge.title: Class Attendance Pilot

summaries.summary:
Build a simple attendance website for a supervised class pilot in week 6.
The intended audience is 40 teachers and 1,200 students; wider use needs school approval and capacity checks.

Keep session opening, ten-minute check-in, automatic teacher lists, manual corrections and CSV export.
Later: statistics, absence emails, native app, QR codes, name search, separate undo and class-management screens.

Use Django, PostgreSQL, shared HTML/CSS pages and small JavaScript files; no React or AI.
Use free school-supported EU hosting and school login, conditional on week-1 confirmation.

Sara owns server rules and data; Adam owns browser behaviour; Yassine owns layouts and acceptance checks.
Students sign in, then enter a session code. Teacher lists refresh every five seconds; codes do not prove presence.

Keep school identity, class membership, sessions, attendance and correction history; copy the class roster when a session opens.
Use invented development records. Keep real records, exports, logs and backups in approved EU locations.

Use school login instead of building password activation and recovery; unresolved login means an invented-data demo only.
Check class access on every server request, enforce the deadline and prevent duplicate records. Protect exports and record corrections.

Use school-style pages for teacher classes, the register, student check-in and the result, plus school-login messages.
Keep names in a stable order, support keyboards and phones, and show saved, failed and outdated states clearly.

Plan 100 of 144 hours: Adam 33/48, Sara 33/48 and Yassine 34/48; protect 44 hours, or 30.6%, as buffer.
These replace overlapping expert estimates and include learning, security and checks. Build in weeks 1–5; week 6 is testing, fixes and demo only.

Real use depends on free approved EU infrastructure, supported school login, supplied class lists and working school Wi-Fi.
Resolve open school questions in week 1. If prerequisites fail, keep the complete demonstration fictional and report real use as blocked.

tasks.title: Gather school answers: pilot or launch, login, class lists, EU hosting and exports, retention, incident contact, Wi-Fi access, attendance proof, school style and weekly availability; arrange teacher reviews (3h)

Check free school infrastructure, EU data locations, school-login support, class-list format and operating owner; agree largest class, peak check-ins, storage needs and five-second updates; set real-use or fictional-demo route (4h)
Learn Django data models, forms, accounts and test structure using invented records (4h)
Learn Django browser integration; set up the shared code repository, local PostgreSQL and setup guide; agree request examples and track scope weekly (9h)
Learn Django templates and sketch four screens, sign-in-first code entry, expired-login recovery, failure messages and teacher fallback; test available host and login addresses on school Wi-Fi (7h)
Create tables and database migrations; validate school-supplied class imports; enforce one attendance record per student and session; supply example responses (6h)
Connect the supported school login, trusted roles and class permissions; configure session protection, request checks and account-based attempt limits; test denied access (5h)
Connect sign-in, sign-out and login error behaviour using agreed responses; preserve typed code through expired login and recheck it afterwards (4h)
Build shared school-style templates and CSS for phones and laptops, including labels, keyboard focus and login messages (7h)
Implement opening sessions, roster copies, expiring codes, server-timed ten-minute check-in and repeat-safe saves; test pure rules and database duplicate protection (5h)
Build student code entry, class confirmation, check-in and confirmed-result behaviour; retain input after failed requests (5h)
Build teacher class selection, session opening and basic five-second register refresh for the halfway demonstration (3h)
Finish student and teacher screen markup: stable register, counts, Pending labels, code, closing time, result states and correction/export controls; review halfway flow with teacher (8h)
Implement teacher corrections with actor, time, old/new status and reason; prevent retries or simultaneous check-ins from overwriting corrections; test these conflicts (3h)
Implement class-restricted CSV export, validate inputs and neutralise spreadsheet-formula cells; test access and hostile text (2h)
Finish automatic updates: show last success and connection errors, pause hidden-page refreshes and preserve row order, focus and unsaved edits (3h)
Connect correction saving and protected CSV download; keep failed edits, confirm saved status and allow another edit to repair mistakes (4h)
Check keyboard use, zoom, readable contrast, phone layouts and empty/loading/wrong-class/closed-session messages; explain teacher-recorded attendance fallback (3h)

Deploy on approved school-supported infrastructure; configure HTTPS, secrets, restricted database access, approved deletion and encrypted EU backups; prove restoration and check storage and agreed peak load (3h)
Check complete browser flows, cross-class denial, expired login, cutoff, repeated requests, correction conflicts and export safety; review software dependencies and fix integration defects (3h)
Run acceptance checks on school Wi-Fi and representative phones/laptops, including dropped connections and teacher fallback; prepare invented demo records and short user instructions (3h)
Retest browser failures and apply final fixes; freeze feature scope and use only approved buffer for remaining defects (2h)
Run final server and recovery checks, fix remaining defects and document whether real use is approved or blocked (1h)
Retest corrected journeys, finish instructions, rehearse and demonstrate all four must-haves with the teacher; record remaining limits (3h)

merge.halfwayDemo: End of week 3: with invented students, a teacher opens a session, an enrolled student signs in and checks in by code, and the register updates within five seconds.

risks.risk: Free EU infrastructure or supported school login is unavailable, or setup exceeds the estimate.
risks.action: Resolve in week 1 with school IT. The estimates assume supported infrastructure and an existing usable login connection. Do not add custom passwords or email links; demonstrate with invented accounts and records if prerequisites fail.

risks.risk: The school expects department-wide launch rather than a supervised pilot.
risks.action: Ask in week 1 what week 6 must prove and how many classes participate. Commit to the complete pilot workflow; wider launch requires approval, an operating owner and measured capacity.

risks.risk: Learning, integration or school delays consume the 30% buffer.
risks.action: Review hours weekly. Remaining capacity is Adam 15h, Sara 15h and Yassine 14h. Confirm weekly availability, especially week 6. Re-estimate after week 1; reduce rollout or keep the demo fictional rather than remove must-haves or security checks.

risks.risk: School Wi-Fi, shared-network login limits or simultaneous check-ins prevent attendance.
risks.action: Ask for largest class and simultaneous class count; agree a measurable load target. Test host and login access early and complete journeys in week 5. Show failures honestly and retain teacher manual attendance.

risks.risk: Wrong-class access, repeated requests or simultaneous changes expose or corrupt records.
risks.action: Check permissions on every request, including refresh and export. Enforce uniqueness in the database, save related changes together and test teacher corrections against student retries.

risks.risk: Exports, logs, login processing or backups violate the EU-only requirement.
risks.action: Ask who approves data use, all storage and processing locations, retention periods, export handling and incident response. Use invented records until approved; exclude personal data from routine logs, protect exports and test backup restoration.

risks.risk: A remote student checks in, or the teacher projects private attendance information.
risks.action: Ask whether teacher review is sufficient evidence of presence. Explain that accounts and codes cannot prove location. Keep the register on the teacher's laptop and share only the code.

risks.risk: Live updates hide failed saves or disrupt teacher corrections.
risks.action: Keep a stable register, preserve keyboard focus and unsaved values, and show success only after server confirmation. Test failed corrections, expired login and interrupted Wi-Fi before the final demo.

The European Union, where the brief requires student data to remain.

Using an existing school account system to establish who a user is.

Exported values that a spreadsheet might treat as executable calculations instead of ordinary text.

Scrambling information so it can only be read with the right key.

The page control currently receiving keyboard input.
A scannable square that can open a website address.

decision.title: First release size

options.name: Supervised class pilot
options.good: Makes the full attendance flow testable within six weeks.
options.bad: Does not establish readiness for the whole department.
options.fit: Fits the team's 144 hours if the school supplies usable identity, roster and hosting arrangements.

options.name: Department-wide launch
options.good: Immediately serves all 40 teachers and 1,200 students.
options.bad: Adds onboarding, support and peak-load uncertainty.
options.fit: Too uncertain to promise with free resources and this time budget.

decision.why: Deliver a complete small pilot, then use its results to decide whether wider release is ready. The department remains the intended audience.
decision.disagreement: If the brief implies that all 1,200 students must use it by day 42, that commitment needs to be reduced or given more resources.

options.good: Adds useful follow-up information.
options.bad: Requires more rules, screens, email setup and testing.
options.fit: Consumes the buffer needed by a small team with limited backend experience.

decision.why: Keep every stated must-have. Defer statistics, email alerts and the native app, as the brief permits. Avoid adding a class-management interface by using school-supplied lists.

decision.title: Application structure

options.name: React frontend and Python API

decision.picked: Django templates and small JavaScript files
decision.why: The must-haves need forms and a changing list. One application gives all three people useful work while keeping integration small.

decision.title: Hosting

options.name: School-provided EU server
options.good: Can provide persistent storage and approved school-network access.
options.bad: Availability, maintenance support and capacity are unconfirmed.
options.fit: Fits free-only only if the school provides it without charge.

options.name: Render free website and database
options.good: Managed deployment with a Frankfurt region.
options.bad: Database expires after 30 days; website sleeps after 15 idle minutes.
options.fit: Fails the continuing-service need and 42-day project timeline.

decision.title: Database

options.name: PostgreSQL
options.good: Supports concurrent writes and database-enforced uniqueness.
options.bad: Needs installation, credentials and backup setup.
options.fit: Sara knows SQL; school IT support would reduce setup risk.

options.name: SQLite
options.good: Simple file-based setup.
options.bad: Concurrent check-in writes can contend; deployment needs persistent disk.
options.fit: Useful for a small demonstration, less suitable for department-wide bursts.

decision.why: Use one database type in development, testing and deployment. Simultaneous class openings justify the modest setup cost.

decision.title: Live teacher list

options.name: Poll every five seconds
options.good: Simple requests with ordinary retry behavior.
options.bad: Updates can lag five seconds and generate repeated reads.
options.fit: About eight reads per second for 40 open teacher lists.

options.name: Persistent push connection
options.good: Changes reach teachers immediately.
options.bad: Adds connection management and deployment complexity.
options.fit: Not justified unless five-second updates are unacceptable.

decision.why: It meets a practical meaning of live within the six-week schedule. Show the last successful refresh so failures are visible.

decision.title: Sign-in for the first release

options.name: School-provisioned Django accounts
options.good: Uses built-in account handling without an external login integration.
options.bad: School staff must verify identities and manage activation and recovery.
options.fit: Conditional baseline with 12 implementation hours explicitly budgeted.

options.name: School single sign-on
options.good: Students reuse their school login; the school handles password recovery.
options.bad: Requires documentation, access and integration work that is not yet estimated.
options.fit: Choose in week 1 if required or supported within the same budget; replace local-account work.

decision.picked: School-provisioned Django accounts, conditional on week-1 agreement
decision.why: Sara confirms one route with school IT and security in week 1. Local accounts require school-verified, single-use, expiring password-setting links delivered through an approved EU school channel, never shared passwords. Recovery uses the same identity checks and invalidates old sessions. Configure Argon2, a deliberately costly password hash, through Django. [Django password guidance](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/5.2/topics/auth/passwords/). Add account-aware temporary login delays and recovery limits …
decision.disagreement: Security must use the same week-1 choice. If neither route fits the budget and school support, keep the demo fictional; do not silently spend the buffer or release incomplete login.

decision.title: Login and account recovery

options.name: School login
options.good: The school handles passwords and recovery.
options.bad: Needs school access and an approved EU-compatible setup.
options.fit: Best use of 144 hours if available in week 1.

options.name: School-email magic links
options.good: No app passwords; a short-lived email link signs the user in.
options.bad: Needs approved email delivery, abuse limits and protection against reused links.
options.fit: Fallback only if free delivery and EU handling are confirmed.

options.name: App passwords
options.good: Does not depend on school login integration.
options.bad: Adds password storage, recovery and support work.
options.fit: Poor fit for six weeks; requires re-estimation.

decision.why: Use the existing school account system if confirmed. Accept only approved department accounts, and obtain roles from trusted school records. Recovery stays with the school.
